This is a long post, but hopefully I've organised my thoughts well enough that it'll go down easy :) stick with it.

Desire is at the root of pretty much everything in our lives, so I think it would pay to explore exactly what desire is.

I think that ultimately, what we all want is to not want. I think that's what desire is - it exists in order to remove itself, like the snake that eats its own tail. When we want to eat, for example, what we really want to do is remove the state of wanting to eat (hunger), and possibly also to placate (remove) our desire to enjoy something delicious.

I think that desire is more fundamental than hedonism, sex and food though; I think it's at the very root of the human experience. One can be overcome/overwhelmed by desire at different levels; being overcome by desire can mean lust, anger, or gluttony, but I think that the ultimate state of being overcome by desire is being in a state of abject terror and existential horror.

Existential horror can arise, for example, when we think of ourselves as tiny and insignificant components of the universe (the famous Carl Sagan "Pale Blue Dot" video illustrates this worldview). What's at the root of this horror? Well, the pale blue dot freakout comprises two main elements: terror at being tiny, and terror at being insignificant. The ultimate logical opposite of the infinitesimal (the infinitely tiny) is the infinitely large, so a desire for omnipresence is the cause of our terror at being tiny. The ultimate logical opposite of insignificance, or impotence, is omnipotence, so a desire for omnipotence is the cause of our terror at being insignificant.

As most of you will recognise, these are traits most often described as "divine", but I don't really want to talk about the Judeo-Christian God here, with all due respect to people's personal beliefs. I believe that these "divine attributes" are the qualities of the universe (or, more accurately, reality) itself. Reality is, of course, omnipresent: there's no place, time, or space which can't be said to be reality. Reality is also omnipotent: I don't use the word omnipotent to mean the primacy of the ego's will, but rather the simple nature of energy. "Power" can be thought of as an illusory misattribution of the transference of energy: a boulder can be said to be powerful if it smashes through a glacier, but this is just a contrivance of language, and particularly of the English language's tendency towards narrative. It would make just as much sense to say that the boulder was a mere vessel for the energy and that it's gravity which is truly powerful, or that the glacier is what holds the power by being the necessary component for the boulder to fulfil its capacity to smash (these are all other examples of contrivances of language - none is more objectively true than the other).

So, existential terror is the same a desire for (for want of a better word) "divinity". I want to make it clear that I don't see this as an egotistical perversion or a shameful psychopathic or narcissistic lust for glory, but rather just synonymous with the plain fact of existential terror (which is something I think most people experience at some point in their lives), born not out of greed, but illusion (as I'm about to explain).

If existential terror is this desire for "divinity", and we have identified divinity as the state of being reality, how does one placate that terror, remove that desire? I believe that this desire comes from an illusion. In order to remove this desire, we would have to "become" reality, but that only makes sense to a mind which has been convinced by ideology (as I would argue we in the modern western world all have) that it isn't already reality. It would be like a dog getting worked up over a desire to be a dog, chasing its own tail.

So if the terrified person desires omnipresence, what about that person's opposite - the "divine" person? The divine person would feel, or know, that they are identical to reality itself (in other words, reality itself is their identity), and so they would be omnipresent. Although I usually feel as though "myself" is located somewhere in my head, I still feel as though that "essence" of myself is present in my arms, legs, fingers and toes. So it stands to reason that a person who understands that the separation of the self from reality is an illusion - a person who feels as though they are a part of reality and not apart from reality - would feel present in all of reality just as I feel present in all of my body.

If the terrified person desires omnipotence, then the "divine" person feels themselves to be a continuous part of nature with all of the potential energy of infinity stored within them, if only by virtue of the aforementioned omnipresence.

If the terrified person desires omniscience, then the "divine" person is somebody who understands the difference between linguistic understanding and fundamental knowledge. While the person who is terrified by what they don't know sees the world as a finite system of systems ready and waiting to be organised into cogent facts, the person who is divine - content, in other words, to live without a desire for omniscience - understands this: language and understanding exist within reality, and so can never encompass it. Reality can't be completely described any more than it can be completely wet, completely hot, or completely solid. You can spend eternity describing a microsecond depending on how many questions you ask ("where were all the atoms, and what were they doing? What is an atom? What do all the different languages of the universe have to say about them? Why?" etc). So if omniscience isn't a complete "descriptive" understanding, what is it? Well, you "know" how to turn photons into light using your eyeballs and brain, and you "know" how to stand up out of a chair, or how to intend to stand up out of a chair, or how to intend to intend to do something. As we've seen, you can't exhaustively describe these actions using language, because infinity is implied within all action, and you probably can't describe them even a little bit, but you still "know" how to do them on some level. In this sense, omnipotence, omniscience and omnipresence are all basically the same thing (I believe an argument can be made for omnibenevolence as well but I'll leave that for another time).

I don't think it's out of the question that a person who is "divine" in this sense would view their ego in the same way that we view our arms and legs. They might "have" an ego, and not feel as though they "are" an ego. Rather, they are reality; the same reality that we all are, making us all, in a very literal sense, one. In the same way that my left and my right hand, although different, are still both a part of the same body, so too are my body and your body part of the same infinity.

This leaves us with two fundamental "aspects": the ego, or the self, and the divine, or reality itself. The ego drives action through desire, and reality is the field of both that action and that desire. The person with divinity is somebody who either: overcomes the illusion of separateness (as in the case of a very wise person), or never had the illusion of separateness to begin with (as in the case of babies and most animals). I'm not suggesting that everyone should be ascetic and godly though - desire, the "force" of the ego, is just as necessary as divinity, because without desire there would never be any action.
